Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- More than 100 countries attending a conference in Dublin, Ireland formally adopted a treaty Friday to ban cluster bombs -- a large, unreliable and inaccurate weapon that often affects civilians long after the end of armed conflict. Cluster bombs are usually air-dropped shells that eject multiple small bomblets to kill enemy soldiers. A document released by Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs says the countries agreed never to use cluster munitions or the explosive bomblets they contain. The countries also agreed never to develop, acquire, retain or transfer cluster munitions. Countries attending the 11-day conference agreed to the treaty Wednesday but formally signed it Friday. The accord calls for a total, immediate ban of the weapons, strong standards to protect those injured by them, contaminated areas to be cleaned up as quickly as possible and for the weapons to be immediately destroyed, he said. Thomas Nash, coordinator of the CMC campaigning organization, said Wednesday: "This is a great achievement for everyone who has been working hard to see the end of 40 years of suffering from these weapons." Though some of the biggest makers of cluster bombs, including the United States, Russia, China and Israel, were not involved in the talks and have not signed the accord, organizers predicted that those nations would nevertheless be pressured into compliance. "Take the United States," Nash said. "Almost all of its allies are here. They've decided to ban these weapons. That's going to make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, for the United States to ever use these weapons again, either on its own or in joint operations." The agreement requires the destruction of stockpiles of the weapons within eight years, he said. Cluster munitions, which break apart in flight to scatter hundreds of smaller bomblets, are what the International Committee of the Red Cross calls a "persistent humanitarian problem." Most of a cluster bomb's bomblets are meant to explode on impact, but many do not. Estimates show the weapons fail to explode on impact between 10 and 40 percent of the time, the Red Cross says. That means unexploded bomblets lie scattered across a target area, often exploding only when handled or disturbed -- posing a serious risk to civilians. Last week, Acting Assistant Secretary for Political-Military Affairs Stephen D. Mull called it "an absolute moral obligation" to rid a battlefield of unexploded ordnance after the battle. But he also predicted that the United States would not agree to any ban. "We think that it is going to be impossible to ban cluster munitions... because these are weapons that have a certain military utility and are of use," Mull said. "The United States relies on them as an important part of our own defense strategy." Instead, he urged that the weapons be regulated "to take humanitarian considerations into account" and that "technological fixes" be pursued that would render them harmless after a battle. During the 34-day war in Lebanon in 2006, the United Nations estimated that Israel dropped 4 million bomblets, 1 million of which may not have exploded, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross. More than 250 civilians and bomb-disposal operators have been killed or injured by them in southern Lebanon since the war ended. Cluster bombs were also used in the 1999 war in Kosovo. Lt. Col. Jim Burke, a military adviser to the Irish Defense Forces said they quickly became a major killer of civilians. In more than 20 countries, according to the ICRC, cluster bombs have created lasting "no-go" areas, rendering them as dangerous as minefields. Laos is the most affected country. Millions of bomblets dropped during the Vietnam War continue to kill civilians more than three decades later. Still, militaries consider cluster bombs important for use against multiple targets dispersed over a wide area, such as tanks or military personnel moving across the landscape. A single bomb containing hundreds of submunitions can cover more than 18 square miles. CNN's Jacqueline Clyne contributed to this report.

# Cluster Bomb Treaty Adopted by Over 100 Nations

(CNN) -- More than 100 countries gathered at a conference in Dublin, Ireland formally adopted a treaty on Friday banning cluster bombs—a large, imprecise, and inherently unreliable weapon that continues to endanger civilians long after conflicts have ended. Cluster bombs are typically air-dropped shells that release numerous smaller bomblets designed to eliminate enemy combatants. According to a document released by Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs, the signatory nations pledged never to use cluster munitions or their explosive submunitions, and further committed to refrain from developing, acquiring, retaining, or transferring such weapons. While the treaty was agreed upon Wednesday during the 11-day conference, it was formally signed on Friday.

The accord mandates an immediate and total ban on the weapons, establishes rigorous standards to protect those affected by them, and calls for the swift decontamination of affected areas and the prompt destruction of existing stockpiles.

Thomas Nash, coordinator of the Cluster Munition Coalition (CMC), described the moment as historic: "This is a great achievement for everyone who has been working hard to see the end of 40 years of suffering from these weapons."

Although several of the world's leading cluster bomb manufacturers—including the United States, Russia, China, and Israel—did not participate in the negotiations and have not signed the treaty, organizers expressed confidence that international pressure would eventually compel these nations toward compliance. "Take the United States," Nash noted. "Almost all of its allies are here. They've decided to ban these weapons. That's going to make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, for the United States to ever use these weapons again, either on its own or in joint operations." Under the agreement, signatory nations must destroy their stockpiles within eight years.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has characterized cluster munitions—which disperse hundreds of smaller bomblets mid-flight—as a "persistent humanitarian problem." Although most bomblets are designed to detonate upon impact, a significant number fail to do so; the ICRC estimates a failure rate ranging from 10 to 40 percent. Consequently, unexploded ordnance remains scattered across target areas, posing a grave and lasting danger to civilians who may inadvertently trigger these explosives.

Last week, Acting Assistant Secretary for Political-Military Affairs Stephen D. Mull acknowledged an "absolute moral obligation" to clear battlefields of unexploded ordnance following combat. However, he indicated that the United States would not join the ban. "We think that it is going to be impossible to ban cluster munitions... because these are weapons that have a certain military utility and are of use," Mull explained. "The United States relies on them as an important part of our own defense strategy." Rather than an outright ban, he advocated for regulatory measures that would "take humanitarian considerations into account," alongside the pursuit of "technological fixes" designed to neutralize unexploded munitions after combat concludes.

The human cost of these weapons was starkly illustrated during the 34-day war in Lebanon in 2006, when the United Nations estimated that Israel deployed 4 million bomblets, as many as 1 million of which failed to detonate, according to the ICRC. In the years since the conflict ended, more than 250 civilians and bomb-disposal personnel have been killed or injured by these remnants in southern Lebanon.

Cluster munitions were similarly deployed during the 1999 Kosovo conflict, where, according to Lt. Col. Jim Burke, a military adviser to the Irish Defense Forces, they swiftly emerged as a leading cause of civilian casualties. The ICRC reports that in more than 20 countries, cluster bombs have left behind enduring "no-go" zones, as hazardous as traditional minefields. Laos remains the most severely affected nation, where millions of bomblets dropped during the Vietnam War continue to claim civilian lives more than three decades later.

Despite these humanitarian concerns, many militaries regard cluster bombs as a vital tool for targeting dispersed forces across expansive areas, such as tank formations or troop movements. A single bomb, releasing hundreds of submunitions, can blanket an area exceeding 18 square miles.

*CNN's Jacqueline Clyne contributed to this report.*

These munitions typically drop from aircraft, releasing numerous smaller explosive devices designed to eliminate military targets. According to documentation from Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs, participating nations pledged to permanently forgo using cluster munitions or their component bomblets. Additionally, signatory countries committed to abstaining from developing, obtaining, holding onto, or transferring these weapons to others.

While the treaty's terms were initially agreed upon during the conference's Wednesday session, the actual signing ceremony took place two days later, marking the conclusion of an 11-day summit. The agreement mandates an immediate and complete prohibition on these weapons, establishes robust protections for victims, requires swift decontamination of affected regions, and calls for prompt destruction of existing arsenals.

Thomas Nash, who heads the CMC advocacy group, remarked on Wednesday that this represented "a great achievement for everyone who has been working hard to see the end of 40 years of suffering from these weapons."

Notably absent from negotiations were several major cluster bomb manufacturers—the United States, Russia, China, and Israel—none of whom endorsed the treaty. Despite this, conference organizers expressed confidence that international pressure would eventually force these holdout nations toward compliance. Nash specifically addressed America's position: "Almost all of its allies are here. They've decided to ban these weapons. That's going to make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, for the United States to ever use these weapons again, either on its own or in joint operations." Under the agreement's terms, nations have an eight-year window to eliminate their stockpiled weapons.

The International Committee of the Red Cross characterizes cluster munitions—which disperse into hundreds of smaller explosives mid-flight—as creating an enduring humanitarian crisis. While manufacturers design most bomblets to detonate upon contact, a significant portion fail to do so. Red Cross data indicates malfunction rates ranging from 10 to 40 percent, leaving battlefields littered with dormant explosives that often detonate later when disturbed by unsuspecting civilians, creating ongoing danger long after conflicts end.

Stephen D. Mull, serving as Acting Assistant Secretary for Political-Military Affairs, acknowledged last week that clearing battlefields of unexploded munitions constitutes "an absolute moral obligation." Nevertheless, he indicated America would decline to join the ban. "We think that it is going to be impossible to ban cluster munitions... because these are weapons that have a certain military utility and are of use," he explained, adding that "The United States relies on them as an important part of our own defense strategy." Rather than an outright ban, Mull advocated for regulatory measures that incorporate "humanitarian considerations" alongside pursuing "technological fixes" to neutralize unexploded ordnance after combat concludes.

The 2006 Lebanon conflict, which lasted 34 days, saw Israel deploy an estimated 4 million bomblets according to United Nations figures cited by the Red Cross—with potentially 1 million failing to detonate. Since that war's conclusion, southern Lebanon has witnessed over 250 civilian casualties or injuries among residents and munitions-clearance specialists.

These weapons also saw deployment during the 1999 Kosovo conflict, where they rapidly emerged as a leading cause of civilian deaths, according to Lt. Col. Jim Burke, who serves as a military adviser to Ireland's Defense Forces.

The ICRC reports that cluster munitions have transformed portions of more than 20 countries into hazardous "no-go" zones comparable to minefields. Laos suffers the worst effects globally, where bomblets dropped decades ago during the Vietnam War continue claiming civilian lives even now, over 30 years later.

Despite these concerns, military strategists value cluster bombs for their effectiveness against spread-out targets like advancing tank formations or troop movements across open terrain. A single munition packed with hundreds of submunitions can blanket an area exceeding 18 square miles.

CNN's Jacqueline Clyne contributed to this report.

# Landmark Treaty Bans Cluster Bombs

More than 100 countries gathered at a conference in Dublin formally adopted a groundbreaking treaty on Friday to ban cluster bombs—weapons long criticized for their inaccuracy and the devastating, long-lasting harm they inflict on civilian populations. The agreement marks a significant milestone in international humanitarian law and represents years of advocacy by human rights organizations and affected nations.

Under the terms of the treaty, signatory countries are prohibited from ever using, developing, acquiring, retaining, or transferring cluster munitions, as well as the explosive bomblets these weapons scatter across wide areas upon detonation. This comprehensive prohibition addresses one of the primary concerns with cluster bombs: their tendency to leave behind unexploded ordnance that continues to kill and maim civilians, including children, long after conflicts have ended.

The agreement goes beyond a simple ban, mandating a total and immediate halt to the use of these weapons. Additionally, signatory nations have committed to undertaking extensive efforts to clean up areas contaminated by unexploded bomblets and to destroy their existing stockpiles of cluster munitions within an eight-year timeframe. This dual approach—prohibiting future use while addressing the legacy of past deployment—reflects the treaty's comprehensive scope in tackling both immediate and long-term humanitarian concerns.

Notably absent from the negotiations and the resulting accord were major producers and stockpilers of cluster bombs, including the United States, Russia, China, and Israel. These countries neither participated in the talks nor signed the treaty, raising questions about the agreement's overall effectiveness given that some of the world's largest military powers remain outside its framework. However, treaty organizers remain optimistic, expressing confidence that mounting international pressure and shifting global norms will eventually compel these nations to move toward compliance, even without formal accession to the agreement.

Thomas Nash, a representative of the Cluster Munition Coalition (CMC), a key campaigning organization behind the treaty, hailed the agreement as a major achievement following four decades of documented suffering caused by these weapons. Nash suggested that the treaty's impact may extend beyond its signatories, noting that it could create significant practical and political complications for non-signatory nations like the United States. Specifically, he indicated that American forces might face difficulties using cluster munitions during joint military operations conducted alongside allied countries that have ratified the treaty, potentially creating an indirect but meaningful constraint on the weapons' continued use even by nations that declined to sign the accord.

# Dublin Conference Adopts Historic Treaty Banning Cluster Bombs

In a landmark moment for international humanitarian law, representatives from more than 100 countries gathered in Dublin, Ireland, this week to formally adopt a comprehensive treaty banning the use, production, and stockpiling of cluster bombs—weapons that have drawn increasing condemnation from human rights organizations and civilian populations affected by their long-term dangers.

The treaty represents years of diplomatic effort, often referred to as the "Oslo Process," which began in 2007 when a coalition of nations, frustrated by the slow pace of negotiations within the United Nations framework, decided to pursue an independent path toward banning these controversial weapons. The Dublin conference marks the culmination of that process, with delegates reaching consensus on the treaty's final text after intensive negotiations.

Under the terms of the agreement, signatory nations commit to never using, developing, producing, acquiring, stockpiling, retaining, or transferring cluster munitions under any circumstances. The treaty also establishes obligations for countries to clear affected areas of unexploded ordnance, destroy existing stockpiles within eight years, and provide assistance to victims of these weapons.

Cluster bombs, which are typically dropped from aircraft or fired from artillery, are designed to break apart in mid-air and scatter dozens or even hundreds of smaller "bomblets" over a wide area. While intended as a military tactic to target broad areas, a significant percentage of these submunitions fail to detonate on impact, leaving behind a deadly legacy that can persist for decades after conflicts have ended. Unexploded bomblets have been responsible for killing and maiming civilians—often children who mistake them for toys or unfamiliar objects—long after the fighting has stopped, in countries ranging from Laos and Vietnam to Lebanon and Kosovo.

Despite the treaty's broad support among the international community, several major military powers notably declined to participate in the Dublin negotiations or sign the resulting accord. The United States, Russia, China, and Israel—all significant producers or stockpilers of cluster munitions—were absent from the agreement, raising questions about the treaty's ultimate effectiveness in curbing the global use of these weapons.

However, treaty organizers and supporters remain optimistic that the accord will still exert meaningful influence on international norms and military behavior, even without the participation of these key states. They argue that the moral and diplomatic pressure exerted by the more than 100 signatory nations—many of which are close allies of the non-signing countries—will make it increasingly difficult for holdout nations to justify the continued use of cluster munitions on the world stage.

Proponents point to the precedent set by the 1997 Ottawa Treaty banning landmines, which similarly lacked participation from several major powers initially but nonetheless succeeded in stigmatizing the use of landmines globally and significantly reduced their deployment even among non-signatory states. Advocates hope the cluster bomb treaty will follow a similar trajectory, gradually building international consensus and making the use of such weapons politically untenable even for countries that have not formally joined the ban.

The treaty is expected to open for signature later this year, with supporters calling on all nations—including those that abstained from the Dublin talks—to reconsider their positions and join the growing global movement against weapons that disproportionately harm civilian populations long after military objectives have been achieved.

# 108 Nations Adopt Landmark Treaty Banning Cluster Bombs

**DUBLIN** — Delegates from 108 countries formally adopted a treaty Friday banning the use, production, and stockpiling of cluster bombs, capping ten days of intense negotiations that supporters hailed as a major victory for civilians in war zones but that several major military powers, including the United States, refused to join.

The agreement, reached at Croke Park stadium after marathon overnight sessions, requires signatory nations to destroy their stockpiles of cluster munitions within eight years and to clear contaminated land within ten years. It also establishes, for the first time in an international arms treaty, binding obligations for states to assist victims of the weapons.

Cluster bombs scatter dozens or even hundreds of smaller "bomblets" over wide areas. Rights groups say a significant percentage of these fail to detonate on impact, leaving de facto landmines that kill and maim civilians — often children — long after conflicts end.

"This is a historic moment for the international community," said Irish Foreign Minister Micheál Martin, who chaired the conference. "We have shown that when states come together with a sense of moral purpose, we can act to save lives."

## Campaigners Celebrate, With Caveats

Representatives from the Cluster Munition Coalition, an umbrella group of nongovernmental organizations that lobbied for the treaty, called the agreement a triumph but stressed the work is far from finished.

"Today the world said no more to a weapon that has terrorized civilian populations for decades," said Steve Goose of Human Rights Watch, one of the coalition's leading voices. "But our celebration is tempered by the knowledge that the world's largest producers and stockpilers have not yet joined us. We will not rest until they do."

Survivors of cluster bomb attacks were among the most emotional voices at the signing ceremony. Branislav Kapetanović, a Serbian de-mining expert who lost both arms and both legs in a cluster bomb accident, addressed delegates directly.

"You have given hope to thousands of people around the world who live in fear of these weapons every single day," Kapetanović said. "Now you must make sure this treaty is not just words on paper."

## Major Powers Stay on the Sidelines

Notably absent from the list of signatories were the United States, Russia, China, Israel, India, and Pakistan — nations that together account for the vast majority of the world's cluster munition stockpiles.

The Bush administration, which sent observers to the talks but did not participate in negotiations, defended its decision not to join the ban.

"Cluster munitions have demonstrated military utility," said a Pentagon spokesman, adding that U.S. forces "make every effort to minimize harm to civilians" and that a blanket ban would put American troops and allied forces at a disadvantage on the battlefield. "We believe the position taken by these countries fails to reflect the realities of the complex, integrated defense relationships that the U.S. maintains with allies and partners around the globe."

U.S. officials also argued that newer cluster munitions, designed with self-destruct mechanisms intended to reduce failure rates, address many of the humanitarian concerns raised by campaigners — an argument that arms control advocates dismissed as insufficient.

"Self-destruct mechanisms fail too, and battlefield conditions are never as clean as manufacturers claim in testing," Goose said. "The only real solution is a comprehensive ban."

Britain, which does maintain a stockpile of the weapons, broke with Washington and signed the treaty, as did several other NATO members, in a move analysts said could increase pressure on the U.S. to reconsider its position over time.

## What Comes Next

The treaty will open for signature in Oslo in December, with formal ratification by individual governments to follow. It will enter into force once 30 countries have ratified it domestically.

Diplomats compared the effort to the 1997 Ottawa Treaty banning landmines, which was similarly negotiated outside the traditional United Nations disarmament framework after major powers blocked progress within it. That treaty, too, was not initially signed by the United States, though it has since been credited with dramatically reducing landmine casualties worldwide and stigmatizing the weapon even among non-signatories.

Campaigners expressed hope that a similar dynamic — a "stigmatization effect" — might eventually pressure holdout nations to change course, even without formal accession to the treaty.

"No country wants to be seen using a weapon that the vast majority of the world has explicitly rejected as inhumane," said one European diplomat involved in the talks, speaking on condition of anonymity. "That reputational cost matters, even to the powers that didn't sign today."

For now, though, the split leaves a fractured global landscape: more than 100 nations bound by a legal prohibition, and several of the world's most heavily armed militaries continuing to reserve the right to use a weapon that the treaty's supporters say has no place on a modern battlefield.

# Convention on Cluster Munitions (2008)

## Overview
The Convention on Cluster Munitions (CCM) was adopted in **Dublin, Ireland in May 2008** and opened for signature in **Oslo in December 2008**. It's often called the "Oslo Process" treaty because it emerged from a diplomatic initiative led by Norway after cluster munitions couldn't gain sufficient restriction through the UN's Convention on Conventional Weapons framework.

## Key Provisions
- **Comprehensive ban** on the use, production, stockpiling, and transfer of cluster munitions
- **Clearance requirements**: Signatories must clear contaminated areas within their territory within 10 years
- **Stockpile destruction**: Existing stockpiles must be destroyed within 8 years
- **Victim assistance**: Establishes obligations for helping survivors and affected communities
- **Definition scope**: Covers weapons that disperse multiple smaller submunitions over an area, which often fail to detonate immediately and pose long-term dangers similar to landmines

## Participation
- Approximately **107-108 countries** participated in the Dublin negotiations
- The treaty ultimately gathered around **94 initial signatories** in Oslo, with more joining over time
- Notable signatories included the **UK, Germany, France, Japan, and Australia**
- It entered into force in **August 2010** after reaching the required 30 ratifications

## Major Non-Signatories
Several major military powers **refused to sign or participate substantively**, including:
- **United States**
- **Russia**
- **China**
- **India**
- **Pakistan**
- **Israel**
- **Brazil**

These countries argued cluster munitions retained legitimate military utility and that the treaty could constrain their defense capabilities without addressing the arsenals of other non-signatory states.

## Caveat
I'd recommend verifying specific figures (exact participant counts, precise timelines) against primary sources like the ICRC or the treaty's official depositary records, as my training data may not capture the most precise details or subsequent amendments/accessions.

# UN Treaty Bans Cluster Munitions Amid Humanitarian Concerns

**Geneva** — Nations gathered this week to address the continued use of one of modern warfare's most controversial weapons: cluster bombs. The Convention on Cluster Munitions, first adopted in Dublin in 2008, continues to serve as the primary international legal instrument banning these weapons, with humanitarian organizations pressing for expanded ratification.

## What Are Cluster Bombs?

Cluster munitions are weapons that release dozens or even hundreds of smaller explosive submunitions, often called "bomblets," over a wide area. Deployed via air-dropped bombs, artillery shells, or rockets, they are designed to disperse across a target zone, making them attractive militarily for hitting dispersed forces or equipment.

However, these weapons carry a severe design flaw: a significant percentage of submunitions fail to detonate on impact. These unexploded remnants effectively become landmines, littering landscapes long after conflicts end.

## The Humanitarian Toll

The human cost of cluster munitions has been staggering. According to monitoring groups including the Cluster Munition Coalition, civilians account for the vast majority of casualties—both during initial strikes and from unexploded ordnance discovered years or even decades later.

Children are particularly vulnerable, often mistaking small, colorful submunitions for toys. Countries including Laos, Vietnam, Cambodia, Lebanon, and more recently Syria, Yemen, and Ukraine have reported ongoing casualties from cluster munition remnants.

Beyond immediate casualties, contaminated land becomes unusable for agriculture, construction, or daily life, trapping communities in cycles of poverty as clearance operations—often slow, expensive, and dangerous—proceed over many years.

## The Convention on Cluster Munitions

Prompted by mounting evidence of civilian harm, over 100 nations negotiated the Convention on Cluster Munitions, which opened for signature in Oslo in December 2008 and entered into force in August 2010. Key provisions include:

- **Comprehensive Ban**: Prohibits the use, production, stockpiling, and transfer of cluster munitions.
- **Stockpile Destruction**: Requires signatory states to destroy existing stockpiles within eight years.
- **Clearance Obligations**: Mandates clearance of contaminated areas within ten years, with possible extensions.
- **Victim Assistance**: Uniquely, the treaty requires states to provide assistance to survivors, including medical care, rehabilitation, and socioeconomic support—not just clearance of ordnance.
- **International Cooperation**: Encourages assistance between wealthier nations and those most affected by contamination.

## Gaps and Ongoing Challenges

Despite the treaty's achievements, significant gaps remain. Major military powers—including the United States, Russia, China, and India—have not joined the convention, arguing the weapons retain legitimate military utility when used carefully.

Recent conflicts have reignited debate. Reports of cluster munition use in Syria, Yemen, and the war in Ukraine have drawn condemnation from treaty signatories and human rights organizations, even as some non-signatory nations continue producing or deploying these weapons.

## Looking Ahead

Advocacy groups continue pushing for universal adoption of the treaty, framing it alongside the Ottawa Treaty on landmines as a model of humanitarian disarmament. For survivors and communities still living amid unexploded remnants, the international debate carries urgent, personal stakes—each unmarked field or roadside representing ongoing risk to life and limb.

As diplomatic discussions continue, the tension between military strategic interests and humanitarian imperatives remains at the heart of the international community's struggle to fully eliminate these weapons from modern warfare.

*This report reflects publicly available information on international humanitarian law and disarmament efforts as of recent years. Readers seeking current, verified statistics should consult primary sources such as the International Committee of the Red Cross, the Cluster Munition Coalition, or official UN treaty documentation.*

# 100+ Nations Agree to Historic Ban on Cluster Munitions in Dublin

**DUBLIN** — In a landmark moment for international humanitarian law, representatives from more than 100 countries reached a formal agreement here to ban the use, production, stockpiling, and transfer of cluster munitions, weapons that have left a devastating legacy of civilian casualties across multiple conflict zones for decades.

The agreement, forged after intense negotiations, marks one of the most significant achievements in arms control since the 1997 Ottawa Treaty banning landmines. Delegates, activists, and survivors gathered in the Irish capital to finalize language that supporters say will save countless lives in future conflicts and accelerate cleanup efforts in regions still contaminated by unexploded munitions.

## A Weapon With a Grim Legacy

Cluster munitions are bombs or artillery shells that disperse dozens or hundreds of smaller submunitions, or "bomblets," over wide areas. Designed to maximize damage against troop concentrations or armored vehicles, the weapons have a notoriously high failure rate—meaning many bomblets fail to detonate on impact and remain live in fields, roadsides, and residential areas long after conflicts end.

The weapons' toll has been felt acutely in Southeast Asia, where American cluster bombs dropped during the Vietnam War era continue to kill and maim civilians in Laos more than a generation later. Cambodia and Vietnam carry similar scars. More recently, cluster munitions were used extensively in the Balkans during the 1990s conflicts and in Lebanon during the 2006 war with Israel, where southern villages were left littered with unexploded ordnance in the war's final days.

"These weapons do not distinguish between soldiers and children," said one campaign representative present at the talks. "A farmer plowing his field decades after a war has ended should not have to fear for his life. That is the reality we are trying to end."

## Voices From the Negotiating Table

Officials who championed the treaty framed it as both a moral and practical imperative.

"Today Dublin has done something extraordinary," said a senior diplomat involved in brokering the agreement. "We have shown that when the international community musters the political will, we can act decisively to protect civilians from weapons whose harm far outlasts any battlefield advantage."

Representatives from humanitarian organizations who had pushed for years for such a ban expressed cautious optimism, tempered by the recognition that major military powers—including the United States, Russia, and China—were notably absent from the negotiations and have not signed on.

"This treaty is not the end of the fight," said a representative from a coalition of disarmament groups. "It is a foundation. Universal participation remains the goal, and we will continue pressing every government, including those not present in Dublin, to reconsider their positions."

Survivors of cluster munition strikes also addressed delegates, offering firsthand testimony of the weapons' long-term human cost. Several described losing limbs or family members to ordnance that had lain dormant for years before detonating.

## What the Agreement Requires

Under the terms reached in Dublin, signatory nations commit to:

- A comprehensive ban on the use, development, production, stockpiling, and transfer of cluster munitions
- Destruction of existing stockpiles within eight years
- Clearance of contaminated areas within ten years
- Assistance programs for survivors and affected communities

The treaty also establishes reporting mechanisms intended to hold signatories accountable for compliance, modeled in part on the framework established by the landmine ban treaty.

## Reactions and Road Ahead

While hailed by disarmament advocates as a watershed moment, the agreement's long-term impact will depend heavily on whether major producers and stockpilers of cluster munitions eventually join. Absent their participation, critics note, the weapons will likely remain in active arsenals and continue to see use in future conflicts.

Nonetheless, supporters argue that the Dublin agreement establishes a powerful new international norm—one that stigmatizes the weapons much as the landmine treaty did, potentially influencing even non-signatory states' battlefield conduct.

The treaty is expected to open for formal signature later this year, with advocates hoping the Dublin agreement will build irreversible momentum toward the weapons' eventual global elimination.

For the survivors and communities still living alongside unexploded ordnance decades after the guns fell silent, the agreement offers something that has long been in short supply: hope that future generations might be spared the same fate.

# Cluster Bomb Treaty Highlights Divide Between U.S. and Allies on Unexploded Ordnance Crisis

**(CNN)** -- More than 100 nations have signed onto an international treaty banning the production, use, stockpiling, and transfer of cluster munitions, a weapons category that humanitarian groups say leaves a deadly legacy of unexploded ordnance long after conflicts end. The United States, however, remains outside the agreement, citing military necessity and questioning the treaty's practical enforceability.

## The Convention on Cluster Munitions

The Convention on Cluster Munitions, which opened for signature in Oslo, Norway, emerged from what diplomats called the "Oslo Process" -- a fast-tracked diplomatic effort launched after cluster munitions drew international condemnation for their use in conflicts including the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war in Lebanon.

Cluster bombs are weapons that scatter dozens or hundreds of smaller submunitions, or "bomblets," over wide areas. Militaries have used them for decades because they can blanket large swaths of territory, useful against troop formations or armored columns. But a significant percentage of these submunitions -- estimates commonly range from 10% to 40% depending on the munition type and terrain -- fail to detonate on impact.

Those "duds" then function essentially as landmines, capable of killing or maiming civilians, especially children, years or even decades after fighting has ended.

Signatory nations, including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and dozens of others, have committed under the treaty to destroy stockpiles within eight years and clear contaminated land within ten years, while also providing assistance to victims.

## Why Washington Has Refused to Sign

The United States, along with other major military powers including Russia, China, Israel, India, and Pakistan, has declined to join the convention. Pentagon officials and administration representatives have offered several justifications:

**Military utility.** Defense officials argue cluster munitions remain a legitimate and, in some scenarios, irreplaceable tool for engaging massed enemy forces over large areas, reducing the need for repeated airstrikes that could otherwise endanger pilots or require more munitions overall.

**Sovereignty and alliance concerns.** Some U.S. officials have expressed concern that a blanket ban could complicate joint operations with allied nations that are signatories, creating legal and logistical ambiguities during coalition warfare.

**Technological alternatives.** The Pentagon has pointed to efforts to develop cluster munitions with lower "dud rates" -- some officials have cited internal defense policy requiring 99% reliability rates for new munitions -- as a way of addressing humanitarian concerns without a total ban.

**Treaty verification.** U.S. officials have also questioned how compliance would be verified and whether nations with poor human rights records would adhere to the treaty's provisions even if they signed it, potentially disadvantaging countries that do comply.

Critics of the U.S. position, including groups like Human Rights Watch and the Cluster Munition Coalition, argue that Washington's stance undermines the treaty's global impact given the size and reach of the U.S. military, and that "reliability" statistics from manufacturers often don't hold up in real-world battlefield conditions of dust, mud, and vegetation.

## Lebanon: A Case Study in Contamination

Lebanon has become one of the most frequently cited examples of the long-term dangers posed by unexploded submunitions. During the 34-day conflict between Israel and Hezbollah, the Israeli military fired an estimated four million submunitions into southern Lebanon, according to United Nations estimates -- a significant portion of them in the war's final 72 hours, after a ceasefire had already been negotiated.

U.N. mine action teams estimated that as many as 1 million unexploded bomblets remained scattered across farmland, orchards, and residential areas in the aftermath. Clearance teams working with the United Nations Mine Action Coordination Centre spent years painstakingly removing ordnance from the region.

Casualty figures compiled by Lebanese and international demining organizations documented hundreds of civilian casualties in the years following the conflict, many of them farmers returning to tend groves and fields, or children who mistook the small, sometimes colorful submunitions for toys or interesting objects.

## Laos: The Longest Shadow

If Lebanon illustrates the immediate aftermath of cluster bomb use, Laos represents its most enduring legacy. Between 1964 and 1973, U.S. forces dropped more ordnance on Laos than was dropped on Germany and Japan combined during all of World War II, according to U.S. government and Laotian government estimates -- much of it in the form of cluster munitions during the "Secret War" conducted alongside the conflict in Vietnam.

Estimates suggest the U.S. dropped more than 270 million submunitions on Laos during that period. Officials with Laotian government clearance agencies and international NGOs estimate that up to 30% failed to explode on impact, leaving tens of millions of live submunitions scattered throughout the country.

More than four decades after the bombing campaign ended, unexploded ordnance continues to kill and injure people in Laos. Government and NGO figures have documented more than 20,000 casualties in Laos since the end of the war, with a substantial share of victims being children, who are sometimes drawn to the small, round "bombies" -- as they are known locally -- while playing or working in fields.

Clearance efforts in Laos have proceeded slowly given the sheer scale of contamination; some estimates suggest less than 1% of contaminated land had been cleared decades after the bombing ended, though international funding for demining organizations has increased in recent years.

## The Path Forward

Advocacy groups continue to press Washington to reconsider its position, arguing that the humanitarian toll documented in Lebanon and Laos illustrates precisely why a comprehensive ban -- rather than reliance on improved "reliability rates" -- is necessary.

U.S. officials, for their part, have indicated openness to discussing cluster munitions policy while maintaining that a full ban is not currently compatible with American military planning.

For residents of contaminated regions in Laos and Lebanon, the debate over treaty language remains secondary to a more immediate reality: decades after the guns fall silent, the ordnance left behind continues to pose a lethal threat to farmers, children, and anyone whose daily life intersects with land still seeded with unexploded munitions.

*This report includes estimates compiled from United Nations agencies, national demining authorities, and humanitarian organizations tracking unexploded ordnance contamination.*
